summary.text: Cross-bedding is layering inside a rock bed that slants at an angle to the bed's main layers, a tilt built in as the sediment settled rather than added later.
It forms as ripples and dunes move downstream: grains climb the gentle upstream side, pile up at the crest, then avalanche down the steeper downstream side.
Because the slanted layers dip in the direction the water or wind was flowing, geologists use them to read the directions of ancient currents.

facts.label: Foreset angle
facts.value: About 34 degrees, the angle of repose

facts.label: Most common in
facts.value: Stream deposits, tidal areas and wind-blown dunes

items.prompt: In sandstone made from ancient river dunes, the slanted layers all dip toward the sunrise. Which way was the old current moving?

options.label: Toward the east
Toward the west
Toward the north
Straight downward

items.explain: Dune cross-beds build up as sand avalanches down the downstream side, so they dip the way the current flowed.

items.prompt: You spot slanted layers inside a flat sandstone bed. What does that tell you about how the sand was laid down?

options.label: It settled out of perfectly still water
It was carried by moving water or wind
It fell as ash from a volcanic eruption
It froze in place under thick glacier ice

items.explain: Cross-bedding forms on the sloping faces of ripples and dunes, which only build up where a fluid such as water or wind is flowing.

items.prompt: Wind keeps pushing sand up one side of a dune. Why do new slanted layers end up on the far side?

options.label: The wind digs sand out of the far side
Rain washes sand back up the near side
Sand piles at the crest, then slides down
Heavier grains sink straight into the crest

items.explain: Grains gather at the crest until it gets too steep, then avalanche down the downstream side, laying down a new slanted layer each time.

items.prompt: Roughly how steep are the slanted layers when they are first laid down on a dune's downstream face?

options.label: About 5 degrees
About 15 degrees
About 80 degrees
About 34 degrees

items.explain: These layers settle at the angle of repose, the steepest slope loose sand holds, which is about 34 degrees from horizontal.

items.prompt: In curved, trough-shaped cross-beds, measuring single slanted layers gives directions that disagree wildly. What gives the true flow direction?

options.label: The steepest single layer in the set
The axis running along the trough
The total thickness of the set
The colour of the coarsest grains

items.explain: Layers in a trough can dip in directions up to 180 degrees apart, so the trough's axis is used to find the real current direction.

items.prompt: A friend sees slanted layers inside a flat-lying sandstone and says later earth movements must have tilted them. Why is that wrong for cross-bedding?

options.label: Sandstone layers cannot be tilted
The layers were tilted by tree roots
The slope formed as the sand settled
The slope comes from later erosion

items.explain: Cross-bedding's tilt is original: the layers were laid down on the sloping faces of ripples and dunes, not bent afterwards.
